title: Jury Selection and Public Data
answer: Jury selection and public data covers the use of openly available records to understand the pool from which a jury is drawn and to prepare for questioning during voir dire. The public data in question includes voter registration lists, property records, court dockets, campaign finance filings, and census figures, all of which are lawful to consult in most jurisdictions. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Jury selection and public data covers the use of openly available records to understand the pool from which a jury is drawn and to prepare for questioning during voir dire. The public data in question includes voter registration lists, property records, court dockets, campaign finance filings, and census figures, all of which are lawful to consult in most jurisdictions. The work sits inside litigation prediction and judicial analytics, where the aim is a defensible picture of the venire rather than a guess about how any single person will vote. It touches both civil and criminal practice, though the constitutional rules differ sharply between them.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The inputs are ordinary public records, often pulled from county websites, state election offices, and commercial aggregators that resell the same data. Processing runs on standard database and spreadsheet tooling, with matching and de-duplication against names and addresses to link a juror record to other sources. Some vendors layer machine learning on top to score or cluster jurors, but the underlying stack is mostly data cleaning, geocoding, and search. Storage and access controls matter because the records are public individually yet sensitive when assembled into a profile.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners build a panel list from the court's source of jurors, then enrich each entry with public records and prior jury service. Analysis is usually descriptive: age bands, neighborhood, occupation, and voting history where that history is public. Statistical models, when used, tend to be simple and are often challenged, because a model that predicts verdicts from demographics invites scrutiny under Batson and its civil analogues. The defensible practice is to use the data to frame questions and identify hardship or bias, not to strike jurors on protected grounds.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The governing constraints are the equal protection rule against discriminatory peremptory strikes, state jury selection statutes, and rules on the use of juror information. Public does not mean unrestricted: many courts limit copying juror lists, forbid contacting jurors, and restrict post-verdict research. Data provenance matters because aggregator records carry errors that can misidentify a person, and a mistaken profile can taint a strike. Attorneys also face professional conduct duties on candor and on the use of investigative services, and any automated scoring should be documented so it can be explained if challenged.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect tighter court rules on juror data scraping and on the disclosure of any algorithm used to rank or strike jurors. Litigants are already testing whether demographic proxies in selection tools violate anti-discrimination law, and those challenges will shape what vendors can sell. Better provenance and audit trails are likely to become a selling point as courts ask how a panel list was assembled. The broader direction is toward transparency: tools that help attorneys ask better questions rather than tools that claim to predict a juror's vote.
